_source: Wording: public/ai4artsed-frontend/src/i18n/en.ts, moved unchanged. Nothing here is rewritten.
Where a page carries no authored text, the wording stands here and only here; the build keeps it, field by field.
Item list: the tab arrays actually rendered in image_lab.vue, latent_text_lab.vue, crossmodal_lab.vue, compare_hub.vue.

names: the label each item carries on the page, from every catalogue in public/ai4artsed-frontend/src/i18n/index.ts; where a catalogue has no string of its own, the string of the frontend's fallbackLocale, as the frontend shows it. name: the handle the tools find an item by.
Built by devserver/scripts/build_platform_items.py. Re-run it after the catalogue changes.
The per-page annotations (what a page is about and what is learned on it) are not in here yet.

Teaching scenarios and the AI-literacy mapping per route: devserver/my_app/knowledge/use_reports.json (the versioned use reports), joined by route at runtime in platform_items.py; not carried in this file since 2026-11-06.

technical.what: Two sets of three stand to choose from: three of today's AI models, or the same family three years apart, 2022, 2023 and 2024. All three compute with the same prompt and the same seed. Besides the sets, the models can also be chosen one by one. At least two models stay selected. To the prompt, the platform also searches for pictures on Wikimedia Commons. The row "Results for this prompt" under the columns shows these finds, with the search term in its header. The platform forms the search term from the prompt.
technical.how: What separates the pictures lies in the differences between the AI models: those you can explore yourselves. Test what the AI models can produce and where knowledge is missing, and look into whether they fall for clichés and fakes. With a prompt that names an occupation, for instance “a nurse at work” from the list "Example prompts", each column shows whom the model draws for it: gender, age, skin, setting. The row from Wikimedia Commons shows, for the same search term, what the archive holds.
technical.brief: Same prompt, different models, different assumptions. Reveals what each model treats as the default human, family, or profession.
technical.technical:
The image models on this surface, in the detail the box on the page leaves out.

SD 1.5 generates the picture by denoising in a compressed latent space, and the prompt goes through one frozen CLIP encoder (Rombach et al. 2022, "High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models", CVPR 2022, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2112.10752). SDXL is built on that construction, with OpenCLIP ViT-bigG beside CLIP ViT-L. Podell et al. (2023, "SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis", ICLR 2024, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2307.01952) give the two denoisers as 860M and 2.6B parameters. Esser et al. (2024, "Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis", ICML 2024, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.03206) then replace the U-Net with a transformer whose blocks carry text and image through the same attention mechanism with weights of their own, trained on rectified flow; SD 3.5 Large has 8.1B parameters in that backbone, beside the two CLIP encoders and a T5-XXL of 4.7B. Black Forest Labs gives the Flux 2 Dev model that runs here as 32B parameters, with a 24B Mistral as its text encoder. For FLUX 3 Image Klein, which runs here too, its model card gives 5.6B parameters for the image transformer and names Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as the text encoder (Black Forest Labs 2026, https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein).

Every parameter count above is the count of the PICTURE-MAKING network alone: 860M and 2.6B are U-Nets, 8.1B is the MMDiT backbone, 32B is the FLUX.2 rectified-flow transformer, 5.6B the FLUX 3 image transformer. The text encoders are counted separately. Read otherwise, 8.1B against 32B compares a backbone with a backbone plus its 24B text encoder.

What varies alongside the model, read off devserver/schemas/configs/output/: SD 1.5 runs 512 x 512, 25 steps, CFG 7.5, sampler euler_ancestral, through ComfyUI. SDXL 1024 x 1024, 30 steps, CFG 7, euler_ancestral, ComfyUI. SD 3.5 Large 1024 x 1024, 25 steps, CFG 5.5, euler, Diffusers. Flux 2 Dev 1024 x 1024, 20 steps, CFG 1, euler, ComfyUI. FLUX 3 Image Klein 1024 x 1024, 16 steps, CFG 1, euler, ComfyUI. All five local configs named here carry an empty negative prompt, so no column suppresses anything the others keep.

The seed: the same number goes to every column whose config has a seed field, and that serves reproducibility. It leaves the starting noise different all the same. The sampler of each column draws its noise through its own generator - ComfyUI's KSampler against a Diffusers torch.Generator - and into a latent of its own shape: 64 x 64 x 4 at 512 x 512, against 128 x 128 x 4 and 128 x 128 x 16 at 1024 x 1024.

One run per model. A difference between two single pictures is not yet a measured difference between two models: the surface is a demonstration, and the model is one of several things that differ between two columns.

Ho et al. (2020) is NO source for the point about the seed, and it was taken out of the references on the page on 2026-09-07. Its "nearly zero mutual information" holds between the endpoint of the FORWARD process and the training datum, and two of the five columns run euler, a deterministic sampler under which the starting noise fixes the picture completely.
technical.reading: Modelle sind nicht neutral — jedes hat eigene Vorlieben (docs/PEDAGOGICAL_CONCEPT.md). Die Reihe mit der festen Startzahl hält alles außer dem Modell fest, sodass sie zeigt, was jedes Modell aus demselben Satz macht. Die fertigen Sätze über dem Eingabefeld sind nach dem Eigenschaften-Katalog der zentralen Presets ausgewählt (UCD-118, Plan Rev. 3); jeder benennt eine beobachtbare Eigenschaft: „a walk in the forest, in the afternoon“ legt die Idiosynkrasie der Modelle offen. „a family at dinner“ überlässt die Menschen dem Modell — Unterbestimmtheit fällt auf demografische Stereotype zurück (Fraser et al. 2023, „A Friendly Face: Do Text-to-Image Systems Rely on Stereotypes when the Input is Under-Specified?“, arXiv:2302.07159; Park 2024, „White Default: Examining Racialized Biases Behind AI-Generated Images“, https://doi.org/10.1080/00043125.2024.2330340). „a street in the evening“ nennt keinen Ort — unterbestimmte Orte bilden überwiegend die Umgebung der USA ab (Basu et al. 2023, „Inspecting the Geographical Representativeness of Images from Text-to-Image Models“, arXiv:2305.11080). „a nurse at work“ neben „a plumber at work“: die Bilder eines Berufs korrelieren mit den US-Erwerbszahlen (Luccioni et al. 2023, „Stable Bias: Evaluating Societal Representations in Diffusion Models“, arXiv:2303.11408), und gewöhnliche Prompts ohne demografische Wörter verstärken Stereotype (Bianchi et al. 2023, „Easily Accessible Text-to-Image Generation Amplifies Demographic Stereotypes at Large Scale“, arXiv:2211.03759). Wer Verstärkung misst, muss Vergleichbares vergleichen: die scheinbare Verstärkung schrumpft, wenn Trainingsbeschriftungen und Prompts dieselbe Verteilung haben (Seshadri et al. 2023, „The Bias Amplification Paradox in Text-to-Image Generation“, arXiv:2308.00755).

technical.what: Every column holds the same prompt, each one in a different language. Two to four languages stand to choose from: the platform's languages and ten further ones, among them Upper Sorbian, Yorùbá and Runasimi. Every selected image model makes a picture from it in every column, one row per model; within a row, all the pictures are made with the same seed. Above each column stands the translation that actually went to the models, and under it, to read along, its way back.
technical.how: Where the way back above a column departs from the prompt as entered, the models in that column received a different prompt. The comparison along a row shows in which languages a model puts the scene of the prompt into the picture and in which something else: landscape, costume, ornament. The same language in two rows shows the difference between the models for this prompt. The box beneath the models names, with sources, what text parts of image models are trained on. A model can set the prompt in the column's language into the picture as lettering.
technical.brief: Same prompt, different languages, different images. This mode shows how language encodes cultural defaults that shape what AI generates.

technical.what: The page takes in a picture, uploaded or drawn here, and offers six perspectives underneath: two descriptions, an art-historical one, an educational-theory one, an ethical one, a critical one. The perspectives range from three sentences ("Neutral description") to a page-long framework with rules of its own ("Critical reading"). The page enters the chosen perspective into the field below as an instruction. Several vision models carry out the instruction; all of them get the same picture.
technical.how: The comparison with the picture separates, in a reading, what it describes, what it interprets and what it adds. A reading can name things missing from the picture, for instance a colour in a black-and-white photograph. The same picture under two perspectives shows what the perspective changes in the reading: the form, and sometimes the claims of fact. The perspective "Critical reading" holds rules of its own for the reading. Whether a model follows them shows in the comparison of the reading with the rule text in the field.
technical.brief: Upload an image and let multiple vision models describe it. Reveals what each model notices, what it ignores, and where descriptions diverge.

technical.what:
1) eSpeak NG (1995): the computer voice from before AI. It works by formant synthesis: rules turn the letters into phonemes, and every phoneme is played as a few resonances. Cf. "speak", Jonathan Duddington, 1995.

2) Piper 1.6.0 (2022): parallel (VITS, 2021: the model forms each sentence in one pass and samples pitch and rhythm anew at every run). Every voice is one model file, trained on a recorded dataset, for most of the installed voices by fine-tuning an English base voice. What can be chosen is which voice model speaks, and the speaker heard is the recorded one. (Michael Hansen, Rhasspy project, 2022; version 1.6.0 published by the Open Home Foundation, 2026) In the German voice "mls", 236 speakers are trained into one model file. Piper speaks with one of them per run. They are volunteers who recorded public-domain books for LibriVox. The research corpus Multilingual LibriSpeech holds their recordings. Under "Speaker", the drop-down names each of them by their number in the corpus, with their index in the file in brackets, and adds gender and the amount recorded as the corpus documents them.

3) Supertonic 3 (2026): 99 million parameters (Supertone, 2026); non-autoregressive (a passage is formed in one pass; the paper the maker names as its architecture, SupertonicTTS, Kim et al. 2025, lists the model without autoregressive inference). A flow-matching decoder over a speech autoencoder (Kim et al., 2025). Ten voices ship with the installed package as style vectors, F1–F5 and M1–M5. This platform mixes them by weighted addition and normalization, e.g. v = (v(F1) + v(F3) + v(M4)) / 3.

4) VoxCPM2 (2026): 2 billion parameters; diffusion-autoregressive (each piece is denoised into place and conditions how the one after it is read, across sentence boundaries too). No parameters; the whole input is read as language; the description of the voice stands in brackets at the start of the prompt and is read as text. (OpenBMB, 2026)
technical.technical:
eSpeak NG (from "speak", Jonathan Duddington, 1995) - the computer voice from before AI. Formant synthesis: rules turn the letters into phonemes, and every phoneme is played as a few resonances. No recording of anybody is in it, which is why it fits into a few megabytes and speaks over a hundred languages.

Piper 1.6.0 (Michael Hansen, Rhasspy project, 2022; version 1.6.0 published by the Open Home Foundation, 2026), VITS (Kim et al., 2021), non-autoregressive (each sentence is formed in one pass, no piece waiting on the one before; longer input is cut at sentence boundaries and each sentence is spoken on its own): every voice is one model file, trained on a recorded dataset, for most of the installed voices by fine-tuning an English base voice (each voice’s MODEL_CARD says which). What can be chosen is which voice model speaks. The speaker heard is the recorded one; pitch and rhythm are sampled anew at every run, which VITS was built for: "a text input can be spoken in multiple ways with different pitches and rhythms" (Kim et al., 2021, abstract).

Supertonic 3 (Supertone, 2026), about 99M parameters, non-autoregressive (a passage is formed in one pass, no piece waiting on the one before; the paper the maker names as its architecture, SupertonicTTS, Kim et al. 2025, lists the model without autoregressive inference; longer input is cut at sentence boundaries into passages of at most 300 characters and each is spoken on its own): a flow-matching decoder over a speech autoencoder (Kim et al., 2025). Ten voices ship with the installed package as style vectors, F1–F5 and M1–M5. This platform mixes them by weighted addition and normalization, e.g. v = (v(F1) + v(F3) + v(M4)) / 3.

VoxCPM2 (OpenBMB, 2026), 2B parameters, tokenizer-free and diffusion-autoregressive (each piece is denoised into place, and what stands there conditions the next): the prompt is read as language rather than as settings. The expression is described in words within the prompt (there are no technical parameters to manipulate emotional expression in this model).
technical.brief: Four text-to-speech systems asked the same sentence side by side - eSpeak NG (1995), Piper (2022), Supertonic 3 (2026), VoxCPM2 (2026) - with an eye to how they stage emotion and gender. What each can be asked for is a different kind of thing: a setting of the formant rules, a choice of voice file trained on a recording, a mixture of ten voice vectors, or a description written into the sentence itself. Every recording stays in the column of the machine that made it.

technical.what: Several image models receive the base prompt once on its own and beside it with a culture or a country named in it: "Yoruba", "Sámi", "Franconian". Every line in the field "Variations (further columns)" replaces the asterisk "*" in the base prompt once and gets a column of its own. The list for the variations offers cultures and six emotions, for a base prompt such as “a person feeling *”. The rows hold the models, the columns the variations, and a model computes in its row with the same seed and with exactly this wording. A further run computes the changed and the empty cells anew, the other pictures stay. The numbers in the note "Stereotype Analysis" come from the studies named there.
technical.how: The field "Variations (further columns)" takes any own word: one's own region, town, community or language. Whoever knows the place can judge whether a model shows a meal, a festival or a greeting from there as it looks there. An expectation written down before the run gets a yes or a no for every picture afterwards. If only one model is selected, five different variations (seeds) are used, so that a range of results can be compared.
technical.brief: A written prompt, put to the chosen image models in one run: as it stands, and again with a culture or a country named in it. Every run includes the prompt without any such addition, and nothing rewrites it on the way to the model.

technical.what: Prompt Interception is the step in which this platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective. Here that step runs several times on the same prompt, once per writing model. Write the prompt, choose the perspective it is to be written through, and choose the set of models that are to write ("Writing models"); one image model puts a picture beside each text. The top row holds the prompt as it was written, and what the image model makes of it with that step left out. The row heads name the models of the set that run in this installation. A change of set adds its rows on top, and the rows so far keep their text and picture.
technical.how: The matter of the comparison is the texts: the form each model sets and names, what it keeps of the prompt, what it drops and what it adds, and its register. The picture beside a text shows what an image model made of this text. The rows of one run compute with the same prompt, the same perspective and the same seed. Where a perspective names a tradition, such as “Bauhaus”, “Literati” or “Renaissance”, the text shows whether a model writes its forms or a cliché of them. The judgement on that comes from knowledge of the tradition.
technical.brief: The same line, written by one model after another

technical.what: Prompt Interception is the step in which this platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective. Here that step runs several times on the same prompt, once per chosen perspective, and one image model makes a picture from each rewritten prompt. The first picture shows what the image model makes of the prompt itself, with that step left out.
technical.how: This surface serves getting to know Prompt Interception: a work goes through several perspectives, and the differences between the results are the matter of the conversation about them. A classical painting dragged onto the field is such a work: for instance Caspar David Friedrich's “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” (1818), written over again through the perspective “Slang”. Every perspective gets a picture for the prompt a language model wrote through it, beside the reference picture. Compared with the work, the new prompt shows what stays under this perspective, what changes and in which register the language model writes. The numbers in the note "Interception Scope" come from the studies named there.
technical.brief: The same template, written through one perspective after another
technical.reading: Die Vorlage ist das WAS, die gewählte Perspektive das WIE. Dieselbe Idee, durch verschiedene Regeln beschrieben, ergibt verschiedene Bilder — die Trennung macht die Regel als Gestaltungsentscheidung sichtbar, die in einem gemischten Prompt unsichtbar bliebe (docs/PEDAGOGICAL_CONCEPT.md, Abschnitt 1). Der Eintrag „forest“ der zentralen Preset-Liste („a walk in the forest, seen through the eyes of a child“, Eigenschaften-Katalog Nr. 4, UCD-118 Plan Rev. 3) lässt sich hier auswerten — in das freie Feld geschrieben; die Auswahl daneben trägt bewusst nur „house“: der Satz benennt sein WAS und darin eine Rolle, die sagt, wer sieht; die Perspektivenliste liefert das WIE.

technical.what: An aesthetic checklist, set property by property, goes with the prompt to a language model, which writes a new prompt from them. Each of the ten properties is a scale of words with a bar. Five chips over the bars, from “best” to “worst”, set the whole checklist at once. Every run adds a picture, and the first picture, "Reference image", stays: the checklist at its neutral word throughout.
technical.how: The properties come from the human labelling guidelines of the rating framework “VisionReward” (Xu et al. 2024), where each of them has one ordered list of words with one of those words marked as the neutral one. The left end of every scale is the end those guidelines count as the good one. Which end counts as the bad one is, according to the note, a decision built into the measurement. According to Guo et al. (2025), named in the note, a model trained on such judgements can adopt the scale as a norm. The comparison of a run with the reference picture shows what the moved properties changed.
technical.brief: One template, an aesthetic checklist set property by property, and a row for every setting
Eight tools for investigating how diffusion models generate images from text. They sort by where they intervene.
technical.hints: Eight tools for investigating how diffusion models generate images from text. They sort by where they intervene. The text encoders turn your prompt into one fixed embedding, and that same embedding then guides all 25 denoising steps. Dimension Explorer, Concept Algebra and Encoder Fusion change the embedding once, before the loop starts, and the Encoder Fusion Workbench sweeps the fusion parameters across three axes. Composable Diffusion stands in both places: it combines what the model returns at each single step, or interpolates between the concepts’ embeddings before the loop starts. Denoising Archaeology and Attention Cartography change nothing and only look. Mean Images leaves the model alone as well and averages many pictures into one. For the two SD 3.5 models it averages the latents of those pictures, before the decoder.

technical.what: An image generator starts from pure random noise and removes that noise step by step, preset at 25, until a scene is left. The platform holds every single one of those steps; the view shows the step at which the "Denoising steps" slider at the picture area stands. After the run the view stands at step 1, the noise. At the right end of the slider it shows the finished picture. Two nets stand at the Backbone to choose from, SDXL (2023) and SD 3.5 (2024), and every run stays under "Runs".
technical.how: The subject of this page is denoising: at every step the net computes from the noisy interim state a less noisy one. According to Choi et al. (2022, in the note), the net settles the coarse features at high noise, the content in the middle and the details at the end, measured by noise level. As a place in the run, this division is a rough orientation, as the note says.
technical.brief: Observe every single denoising step.
technical.reading: Early steps: Global composition — basic structure, color distribution, layout planning. Middle steps: Semantic emergence — objects become recognizable, shapes crystallize. Late steps: Detail refinement — textures, edges, fine patterns. The transitions are gradual, and the three zones are working coordinates, not verified boundaries: Choi et al. (2022) hypothesise a coarse / content / clean-up division, but they locate it by noise level, not by step number, and they measure it during training, not in a generation run. Particularly revealing: The very first step does not show fine-grained pixels, but colorful patches. This is because the noise is generated in latent space (128×128 at 16 channels), not in pixel space. The VAE translates each latent pixel into an ~8×8 pixel patch — even pure Gaussian noise becomes coherent color clusters. The computation runs in this compressed space throughout, rather than on individual pixels.
technical.technical: Two backbones run here: SD 3.5 Large, a rectified-flow transformer whose one scheduler is FlowMatchEuler, and SDXL, a U-Net whose scheduler is picked from a list. SD 3.5 additionally carries a shift, which spreads the steps over the noise scale; its own scheduler config sets that to 3.0. 25 steps are preset. At each step the current latent vectors are decoded through the VAE (Variational Autoencoder), which translates the mathematical latent space into pixels. The latent representation is 128×128 across 16 channels — each latent point corresponds to a patch of about 8×8 pixels in the image. This is why even the first step shows colour clusters instead of fine pixel noise: the VAE translates random 16-dimensional vectors into coherent colour fields. The view shows the noisy intermediate state decoded through the VAE, rather than the model's prediction of the finished image — Ho et al. (2020) show that prediction in their own figures.
technical.hints: Observe every single denoising step. Diffusion models don't draw left-to-right — they work everywhere simultaneously, from rough shapes to fine detail.

technical.what: An AI model generates many images from one prompt, and the page averages them into one mean image. The page computes two means per model. The first is the mean of the images generated from English variants of the prompt: the first variant is the prompt itself, the further ones a language model writes with the same content in other words. Together they are as many as the setting "Images per cell" says. The second is the mean of the images generated from the prompt as entered on randomly varied starting seeds. The models are selectable, one row each; both columns always stand. Under "View" in the left column, three views stand to choose from: the mean, the single images as a contact sheet and a relief of the mean. For the two SD 3.5 models the page takes the mean before the decoder: it averages the latents of the pictures and decodes once. For the other models it averages pixel by pixel, and each row says which.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the mean of many images of one AI model, generated from variants of one prompt or from one prompt on different seeds, in a comparison of several models. The comparison serves the exploration of visual clichés, prejudices and other forms of the statistical production of ‘normality’. What stays in the mean is what stood in the same place in every one of the pictures.
technical.brief: Many generated images, from rewordings of one prompt or from one prompt on different seeds, averaged into one picture. For the two SD 3.5 models the mean is taken before the decoder, and each row says which mean it shows.
technical.reading: Die promptFixed-Achse hält den Satz fest und wandert mit den Startzahlen: was im Mittelbild stehen bleibt, ist der Effekt des Prompts, nicht der einer einzelnen Startzahl. Für die Sätze der zentralen Liste (Eigenschaften-Katalog, UCD-118 Plan Rev. 3) heißt das — das Feld nimmt jeden Satz an, die Auswahl daneben trägt nur „house“ und „street“: „friendship“ und „loneliness“ sind abstrakte Begriffe ohne jede weitere Angabe — das Mittel vieler Bilder zeigt das eine Klischee, in das das Modell den Begriff übersetzt (docs/PEDAGOGICAL_CONCEPT.md: „Abstrakte Konzepte werden oft in Klischees übersetzt“; die DIM-Metrik des DIMCIM-Rahmens beziffert, wie wenig die Erzeugung ohne ausdrückliche Angabe variiert: Teotia et al. 2025, „DIMCIM: A Quantitative Evaluation Framework for Default-mode Diversity and Generalization in Text-to-Image Generative Models“, arXiv:2506.05108). „a family at dinner“ überlässt die Menschen dem Modell, „a street in the evening“ den Ort — Unterbestimmtheit fällt auf Defaults: demografische Stereotype bei Trait-Wörtern ohne demografische Angabe (Fraser et al. 2023, arXiv:2302.07159; Park 2024, https://doi.org/10.1080/00043125.2024.2330340), die Umgebung der USA bei Orten ohne Ortsangabe (Basu et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.11080). „a nurse at work“ und „a plumber at work“ zeigen im Mittel die Lesart, in die das Modell für einen Beruf fällt (Luccioni et al. 2023, arXiv:2303.11408; Bianchi et al. 2023, arXiv:2211.03759).

technical.what: After "Generate + Analyze" the image model (SD 3.5 Large) generates an image for the prompt. In the left column, the same prompt stands once more, split into single words: for a clicked word, the page draws a colour patch over the image exactly where this word had the most influence in the computation; several words carry several colours. The view follows further settings: the computation step on the slider, the layer within it on the network depth (shallow, middle, deep or all three), and the decomposition of the prompt on the text-encoder buttons above the words, one of the two that the model uses side by side, or both.
technical.how: A colour patch is the cross-attention of a word's tokens, recorded at three layers and at every computation step of the run. The shape of a named thing can appear in the deep layer. The shallow and the middle layer can show, for the same word, a colour patch over the whole picture.
technical.brief: For each word in the prompt, a heatmap overlay on the generated image shows WHERE in the image that word had the most influence.
technical.reading: The denoising step slider shows WHEN in the 25-step generation process you are viewing attention. Early steps show rough layout planning, late steps show detail assignment. The network depth selector shows WHERE in the transformer attention is measured: shallow layers (near input) show global composition planning, middle layers semantic assignment, deep layers fine-tuning. Both axes are independent — it is worth systematically exploring different combinations.
technical.technical: SD3.5 uses an MMDiT (Multimodal Diffusion Transformer) with joint attention: image and text tokens attend to each other across 24 transformer blocks. We replace the default SDPA processor with a manual softmax(QK^T/√d) processor at 3 selected blocks to extract the text→image attention submatrix. Maps are 64x64 resolution (patch grid), upscaled to image resolution via bilinear interpolation. SD3.5 has three text encoders — CLIP-L (BPE, 77 tokens), CLIP-G (BPE, 77 tokens) and T5-XXL (SentencePiece, 512 tokens); two of them can be toggled here to see how different tokenization strategies affect attention.
technical.hints:
For each word in the prompt, a heatmap overlay on the generated image shows WHERE in the image that word had the most influence. This reveals how the model spatially distributes semantic concepts.

e.g. A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen.

Click one or more words. Subword tokens (e.g. "Ku"+"gel") are automatically combined. Multiple words appear in different colors.

Diffusion models generate images in 25 steps from noise to image. Early steps establish rough structure, late steps refine details. This slider shows what the model attends to at each step.

At every denoising step, the signal passes through all 24 transformer layers. Shallow layers (near input) capture global composition, middle layers semantic assignment, deep layers (near output) fine details. Both controls are independent: step = when in the process, depth = where in the network.

SD3.5 uses two text encoders with different tokenization. CLIP-L uses BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding), T5-XXL uses SentencePiece. Compare how both encoders process the same prompt and which image regions each one steers.

technical.what: Imagine that an AI model is a large room full of picture elements (sound elements, and so on). This room is huge, but precisely ordered. This is about disturbing that order and reaching places in this room that are impossible to reach with a normal prompt. What comes out are pictures and sounds that bring together everything the model has learned in a completely different way. The results almost always have to do with your prompt, but are literally “out of place” (German “verrückt”, which also means “crazy”). Three text encoders of the image model encode a prompt into a table of 589 rows: a CLIP block of 77 rows above a T5 block of 512 rows. Under the heading "Conditioning table" stand the drawing of this table and the sliders a, b and c: a is the factor on the CLIP block, c the one on the T5 block. With the factor b the page adds the first 77 rows of the T5 encoder into the CLIP block as well. The sliders' scale is uneven: the display rises from 1 to 22 over half of the slider's travel, and the ends stand at −75 and 75.
technical.how: A row that holds both encodings at once lies outside the states the model was trained on. At another value of b and the same seed, the model can change the style, the composition and the objects of the picture.
technical.technical: The arithmetic runs in ComfyUI in the node AI4ArtsEdSD3ThreeFactors (comfyui_nodes/ai4artsed_sd3_conditioning.py), on the parts the encode node of the same family delivers for the prompt: rows 0–76 receive a · CLIP + b · T5[0..76], the rows from 77 on receive c · T5, in float32, nothing clamped. T5 runs at 512 rows (T5TokenizerOptions, min_length 512, devserver/schemas/engine/comfyui_chunk_support.py) or at the prompt’s own length past that. The layout of the block is the fourth parameter, t5_rows: full, rows 0–511 under the CLIP block, a table of 589 rows, or tail, rows 77–511 alone, a table of 512 rows, the layout of the earlier Surrealizer, in which T5’s rows 0–76 reach the model only as the b-fold addend inside the CLIP block. The pooled vector, CLIP-L’s 768 and CLIP-G’s 1280 numbers joined, is the fifth parameter, pooled. Under clip the node hands it on as the two encoders compute it; under zero it hands on zeros of the same shape, which is what ComfyUI itself assembles for the vector when it runs without a CLIP encoder (comfy/text_encoders/sd3_clip.py). The three factors act on the table; the vector passes whole. The negative prompt passes through a second node of the same kind under the same five parameters; an empty negative is the encoding of the empty string. (1, 0, 1, full, clip) is the sequence and the vector as ComfyUI assembles them on its own; (1 − α, α, 1, tail, clip) is the earlier node AI4ArtsEdSD3Fusion under legacy at α, bit for bit, which is what the three Surrealization fields send. Inside the model the whole table passes through one linear layer to the transformer’s width, the same weights for every row, and position encodings are added to the image patches only (Esser et al. 2024, section 4, Figure 2), so a text row’s place in the table plays no part in the computation; a T5 row added into a CLIP row is a sum at that layer’s input. The model reads the pooled vector apart from the table: embeddings of the timestep, the step of the run the model is at, and of this vector are the inputs to the modulation mechanism (Esser et al. 2024, section 4), which every transformer block of the model carries (comfy/ldm/modules/diffusionmodules/mmdit.py), so that zeros in its place change that modulation in every transformer block and leave the table as it is. Esser et al. (2024, “Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis”, ICML 2024, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2403.03206) describe the assembly in appendix B.2, the CLIP rows zero-padded along the channel axis to 4096 and concatenated along the sequence axis with the T5 rows; the training with each encoder set to zero independently at 46.4 % (B.3); and the ablation without T5 in section 5.3.3, with win rates against the full model of 50 % for aesthetics, 46 % for prompt adherence and 38 % for written text. In the paper the T5 context has 77 rows; ComfyUI runs T5 at 512 rows here. CLIP-L is the text encoder of Radford et al. (2021, “Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision”, ICML 2021, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2103.00020), CLIP-G that of the OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14 of Cherti et al. (2023, “Reproducible Scaling Laws for Contrastive Language-Image Learning”, CVPR 2023, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2212.07143), both trained on image–caption pairs; T5-XXL is the encoder of Raffel et al. (2020, “Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer”, JMLR 21, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1910.10683), trained on text alone.
technical.brief: Three factors on the conditioning table of Stable Diffusion 3.5: a on the CLIP block, b for T5’s rows 0–76 added into it, c on the T5 block.

technical.what: After "Analyze" (▶1) the image model generates one picture each for the prompts A and B at the same seed. At the same time the page ranks the numbers (dimensions) of B's text embedding by the size of their difference to A, as a list with rank, name and bar. After ▶2 the image model generates A once more into the middle column, with the dimensions of a chosen range of ranks taken from B. The page compares the embedding of one encoder, chosen at the "Encoder" chips, and with the encoder the number of dimensions changes.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the numbers that a text encoder makes of a prompt. A larger range of ranks from B can move the picture for A towards B. What moves there can be the composition of the picture.
technical.brief: Compare two prompts and discover which embedding dimensions encode the semantic difference.
technical.reading: Each bar represents one embedding dimension. The length shows how much that dimension differs between prompt A and B. Dimensions with large differences are the most likely carriers of the semantic change. But note: embeddings are distributed — often multiple dimensions together are needed to produce a visible change.
technical.technical: SD3.5 uses three text encoders: CLIP-L (768d), CLIP-G (1280d) and T5-XXL (4096d). You can probe each individually. The difference is computed as mean absolute deviation across all token positions: mean(abs(B-A), dim=tokens). The transfer replaces selected dimensions across all token positions simultaneously.
technical.hints: Compare two prompts and discover which embedding dimensions encode the semantic difference. Selectively transfer individual dimensions to see how they affect the image.

technical.what: Three prompts stand in the calculation A − B + C: the page subtracts the text embedding of B from that of A and adds that of C. After "Compute", the picture for A alone stands in the column "Reference (Prompt A)" and the one for the sum in the column "Result (A − B + C)", at the same seed. The weights of B and C stand in the "Advanced settings" as "Subtraction scale" and "Addition scale", from 0 to 3. The calculation runs on the embedding of one encoder, chosen at the "Encoder" chips.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the calculation with embeddings, which the page calls vector arithmetic. One test is “king” − “man” + “woman”. In the result picture, features of the reference picture can stay and others can change. At a larger "Addition scale", the style of the result picture can also detach from the reference picture.
technical.brief: Apply the famous word2vec analogy to image generation: King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen.
technical.reading: On the left you see the reference image (prompt A only, same seed). On the right, the algebra result. If the analogy works, the right image should show concept A but with the semantic change B→C. Example: "Sunset at the beach" − "Beach" + "Mountains" ≈ "Sunset over mountains". The L2 distance shows how far the result has moved from the original. — Is the operation commutative? No. Subtraction of B and addition of C happen relative to vector A. The direction B→C only makes sense in the context of A: "King − Man" removes the "male" directions from the King vector, "+ Woman" adds the "female" directions — the result lands near "Queen". C is not surgically placed where B was removed; it is simply added. That this still works shows that semantic relationships are encoded as consistent linear directions in the vector space.
technical.technical: The algebra is performed on the selected encoder embeddings: CLIP-L (768d), CLIP-G (1280d), T5-XXL (4096d), or all combined (589 tokens × 4096d). The same operation is also applied to pooled embeddings (2048d). Both images use the same seed for fair comparison.
technical.hints: Apply the famous word2vec analogy to image generation: King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen. Three prompts are encoded and algebraically combined.

technical.what: The image model generates one picture from two or more concepts, each a prompt of its own with its own weight. A positive weight adds the concept ("AND"), a negative one subtracts it ("NOT"). The place of composition stands at the "Combination" chips: "In the embedding", once at the start, or "In the denoiser", at every step. With "In the embedding", the mix of the embeddings with a negative weight can give a vector from which the model computes a noise picture.
technical.how: The subject of this page is composition: what dominates in the picture, what recedes, what is left out and how the parts are joined. The thing a concept under "NOT" names can be missing from the picture, a window for instance.
technical.brief: Instead of encoding your entire prompt as one monolithic vector, each concept gets its own transformer pass during denoising.
technical.technical: Based on Liu et al. (2022), Eq. 11 (conjunction) and Eq. 15 (negation). Each concept is encoded with all three SD3.5 encoders (CLIP-L, OpenCLIP-G, T5-XXL) independently. The custom denoising loop calls pipe.transformer() once per concept per step. In the denoiser the weights are read in one of two ways. With "normalize" on, they are shares of the CFG value: the total guidance stays at CFG, so every concept you add makes each individual share smaller. With it off, each weight is that concept’s own guidance temperature, v = CFG × weight, and a negative weight is the NOT operator — algebraically identical to the paper’s eps_u + w×(eps_a - eps_b). A negative weight switches normalization off automatically, because a mixture with signs has no meaning. In the embedding neither reading applies: the concepts are interpolated there, so a weight acts through its ratio to the others, and with three or more concepts the order they stand in acts as well. VRAM: model weights are shared across passes; only activations vary. With 4 concepts, generation takes roughly 4x longer than standard (each step needs 5 transformer passes instead of 2).
technical.hints:
Instead of encoding your entire prompt as one monolithic vector, each concept gets its own transformer pass during denoising. Each one then adds its own pull on the image — or, with a negative weight, subtracts it.

A weight above 0 adds the concept (AND). A weight below 0 subtracts it (NOT) — which is not the same as putting it in the negative prompt. In the embedding only the RATIO of the weights acts: the share the next concept gets is w2/(w1+w2), and multiplying every weight by -1 changes nothing, so 1.00 and -2.00 give what -1.00 and 2.00 give. Two weights of one sign keep that share between 0 and 1 and the result between the concepts. Two weights of different signs send it outside, and the result then turns past the concept whose weight is larger without its sign.

Normalization is off while a concept is negated: a mixture with signs has no meaning, and each weight then acts as its own guidance strength in the denoiser (CFG × weight). It is off in the embedding as well: the run interpolates from one concept towards the next there, so a weight acts through its ratio to the others and there is nothing to normalize.

technical.what: After "Run sweep" the image model generates a grid of pictures from one prompt at one seed, one picture per cell. In the preset, the columns are the chosen fusion strategies ("X · columns") and the rows the denoising windows ("Y · rows"), and in each cell the fusion of the encodings of CLIP (CLIP-L and CLIP-G) and T5 acts in the steps its window covers. The button's title counts the cells: with all five strategies and three windows, that is 15 pictures. The text behind "T5 expand" goes to the T5 encoder alone and is the same in every cell.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the moment in the denoising at which this fusion acts on the picture. The formula in the block "Fusion formula (active)" and the strength α from the "Advanced settings" give the weights of a cell: with "Centered Fade" at α = 20, the weight on CLIP (w_C) stands at −19 and that on T5 (w_T5) at 20.
technical.brief: Assign any parameter to each axis and give it a value list: X = columns, Y = rows, Z = the drive-through slider.
technical.hints: Assign any parameter to each axis and give it a value list: X = columns, Y = rows, Z = the drive-through slider. Everything else stays constant. Each cell is one generation; scrub Z to move through the third dimension.

technical.brief: Representation Engineering, comparative model archaeology, and systematic bias analysis.
technical.hints: Representation Engineering, comparative model archaeology, and systematic bias analysis: Three research-based tools for investigating language models.

technical.what: A language model from the "Model" list continues the prompt three times, in the columns "← against the arrow", "· no arrow (reference)" and "→ with the arrow". Each contrast pair contributes the difference of the model's states between its two sentences, and the arrow is the direction these differences have in common (Zou et al. 2023, in the note). While the model writes, the platform adds a multiple of this direction (the strength on the slider) to the middle layer's output at every token in the column "→ with the arrow", and subtracts it in the column "← against the arrow". With a single pair the steered text can lose coherence in both directions and repeat itself.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the intervention in the inside of a language model: a direction that the platform adds to the model's states while it writes, or subtracts from them. An answer the model gives in the column "· no arrow (reference)" it can evade or replace with another under the direction.
technical.hints:
One axis, straight under the drawing, and it holds a distance from 0.5 to 3 with no sign: both directions run at every press and stand as the two outer columns (“against the arrow”, “no arrow”, “with the arrow”). It starts at 1.5, which tips the answer on the first press. The strength counts in pair-differences along the direction, so 1 is one pair’s worth of push; 0.5 to 2 is the usable band, and above 2 repetition and nonsense take over. In the middle column nothing is added at all — that is the model left alone, and it is there to read the other two against. Each press adds a row to the grid on the right: three cells from one reading and one seed, so two cells side by side differ in the push and in nothing else. The row keeps the prompt it was started with, and says once how hard it pushed and which layer it used.

Three pairs, editable, numbered, and each should differ in one thing. Three is also the ceiling: the button that adds one is gone at three. Once a run has been out, the pairs stand a second time as a drawing under the fields — one grey arrow per pair, each numbered, at the angle its difference has to the direction they share, and one green arrow for that shared direction, which is the one that goes into the writing. Arrows close together mean the pairs differ in the same thing; a wide fan means they differ in several, and the reading keeps only what they have in common. The arrangement is a PROJECTION and not a hand-drawn one: three differences stand at three angles to one another, and three rays from one point on a flat sheet have two free parameters, so a flat picture can hold two of the three angles at once. The plane drawn is the one the reading itself picks out — along the shared direction and across it — and the share of the spread that plane keeps comes back with every run. All arrows are drawn the same length, because a length here would say something about the drawing rather than about the pairs. The weights of the model stay as they are throughout: both the reading and the push happen while the model runs. Swapping a pair’s two sentences costs the measurement nothing — the direction is an eigenvector of a sum of outer products, and flipping one difference leaves its outer product as it was — it turns that one arrow around.

The layer is fixed at the middle of the stack and has no control on the surface. Depth decides what the same push changes: early layers still hold the words themselves, the last ones already hold the next word, and the middle is where a claim stands as a claim — so the middle is the one setting that produces something legible, and the others are settings that waste a run. It is taken from whatever model is chosen, so it follows the depth of that model’s stack; each row of results reports the number it used. An axis for it stood on the surface until 2026-08-25 and was removed.

technical.what: If an AI model carries prejudices, that can become unpleasant or even dangerous, because it often makes decisions, or prepares decisions — for example AI that is used by the police. On this page you can find out for yourselves whether language models carry prejudices. None of these questions is decidable, which is why “cannot be answered” is always the right answer. Still, the language models sometimes pick one of the other answers. Find out whether they then tend to pick the answer that matches the prejudice, or the other one. If a language model decides for the prejudice more often, its “bias score” under the graph goes up. The questions come from the “Bias Benchmark for QA dataset” (Parrish et al., Findings of ACL 2022; data CC BY 4.0 from github.com/nyu-mll/BBQ). Every run draws a fresh random sample of 60 out of the 2,836 open questions of that category.
technical.hints: The 2,836 above is the figure for Gender identity. Every category holds a different number of open questions — twice its situations: Age 1,840, Disability status 778, Nationality 1,540, Physical appearance 788, Race / ethnicity 3,440, Religion 600, Socio-economic status 3,432, Sexual orientation 432, Race x gender 7,980, Race x socio-economic status 5,580. The sample is always 60. Which of the three answers counts as the biased one is not decided by this platform: it comes with the data, per example, and it is polarity-specific — for one question the annotation points at the stereotyped group, for its counter-question at the other one. The bias score follows BBQ's own arithmetic and is scaled by how often the model named anyone at all, so 0 means nothing was measured, not that all is well. Under the score stands the median of every model series ever measured on this installation, from the second series on. At the kids safety level four of the eleven categories are offered — age, socio-economic status, nationality, disability — and within them the situations that turn on drugs, alcohol, violence, weapons, crime, terror, mental illness or sex are kept back, as whole situations and before the draw. The open questions a run can reach there are therefore fewer than the figures above: Age 1,124, Socio-economic status 2,868, Nationality 620, Disability status 382. Below the open level — at kids and at youth alike — six situations are kept back in every category: an autistic classmate mocked as weird, the ethnic body-odour trope, the submissive girlfriend or wife, being ranked by looks, same-sex marriage held against a religious conviction, and racism named as one of the two people's deed (858 of 14,623 situations, 5.9 %). Nothing is removed from the benchmark itself; the open level sees all of it.

technical.brief: Pronoun reference versus stereotype
Same message with three different system prompts. Shows how invisible instructions reshape the same AI into different personalities.

technical.what: One message goes, under one system prompt and one randomness setting, to three language models, one per column from the "Model" list. The list names for the models country, year and size, and whether they compute locally. The field "System Prompt" shows the text of the chosen preset and stays editable.
technical.how: The matter of the comparison is what a language model says, what it leaves out or declines and how it says it: register, hedges, lists, the wording of a refusal. System prompt and randomness hold for all three columns; the system prompt stands open in the field, the randomness on the "Randomness" slider. Three models from three countries on the same question show whether one declines or redirects, and in which words. A local model computes on this installation's server, a cloud model at its provider.

technical.what: The chosen tokenizer ("Tokenizer" chips) cuts the text in the field into tokens, and the page shows each piece numbered, anew at every keystroke. The line below names the number of tokens, the size of the vocabulary and the model's window. A single character, such as “집”, can fall into several pieces, which the page all shows as this character. After ▶ a language model translates the sentence into the eleven languages of the platform, and the page cuts each version.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the cost of a language in tokens: the same sentence costs a different number in each of the eleven languages. For the speakers of an expensive language this means less room in the window and more computing time for the same sentence.

technical.brief: Sound from latent spaces: t5gemma embedding manipulation, image-guided audio generation, crossmodal transfer

technical.what: An audio model generates from the prompts in "Prompt A (Base)" and "Prompt B (Optional, for interpolation)" a sound of twelve seconds, which the page loads into the "Looper / Sequencer" on the right. The slider α mixes the text embeddings of the two: its label names −1 as A alone and 1 as B alone, and on opening it stands at −0.17, close to A. The fold "Dimension Explorer" shows the numbers of the embedding as a strip of fine bars, sorted by the difference between A and B: a drag on a bar sets an offset, and after "Apply and regenerate" the audio model generates the sound anew with it.
technical.how: The subject of this page is the numbers that the text encoder T5Gemma makes of a prompt, and the sound the audio model generates after a change to them. The axes in the fold "Semantic Axes" are directions between word pairs, such as "noise ↔ music (d=2.058)", each with a slider from 0 to 1.
technical.hints:
Length of the generated clip. Below about eleven seconds this model produces malformed audio, so a short clip tells you more about that than about the prompt.

Denoising steps. This model is distilled for eight — more is not better here, mostly just slower.

Classifier-Free Guidance. Guidance is trained into this model, so at 1.0 it is switched off entirely and the negative prompt has no effect at all.
technical.brief: Direct manipulation of Stable Audio 3's t5gemma conditioning space (768d).

technical.what: An audio model generates a sound of up to eight seconds from a picture, a text, or both. The picture stems from an upload, the text from the field "Text prompt (optional)".
technical.how: The subject of this page is the sound an audio model generates for a still picture. According to the title of its source (Cheng et al. 2025, under the settings), the model was built for giving sound to video.
technical.brief: Image and text enter the same network as separate signals — the image is not translated into language, both guide sound generation simultaneously. The model was jointly trained on video and audio, learning direct associations between what is seen and what is heard. Up to 8s, 44.1kHz, ~1.2s compute time. (Cheng et al., CVPR 2025, doi:10.48550/arXiv.2412.15322)

technical.what: An audio model generates a sound of ten seconds for an uploaded picture, adjustable up to 30. In the guided steps ("Guided steps") the picture's embedding in the shared embedding space of ImageBind (Girdhar et al. 2023, in the reference) pulls the generation of the sound towards the picture, with the strength from "Guidance strength". The card of a run names the settings and the number "Cosine similarity (image-audio proximity)": the similarity between the picture and the finished clip in the same space. A "Base prompt (optional)" gives the audio model a text in addition, and with the field empty the picture is the only input.
technical.how: The subject of this page is a measure for the fit of sound to picture. The measure is the cosine similarity of the embeddings of picture and clip in this space.
technical.brief: Gradient-based steering during the Stable Audio 3 denoising process. ImageBind provides a shared 1024d space for image and audio — the gradient of the cosine similarity guides audio generation towards the image embedding.
Original and re-enactment. What can an AI hear, what can it understand of music, and what does it sound like when it rebuilds that? Here you are the original and the AI is the re-enactment.

technical.what: This is about extending the image model Stable Diffusion 3.5. The model itself cannot be changed, but a LoRA model can be added to it: what is learned is not the model again but a small number of additional values, which shift the output towards your images as soon as your trigger word stands in the prompt. Before training, a captioning model looks at every uploaded image and writes down what it recognises — so what a machine recognised takes part in deciding what is learned.
technical.how: Three things can be learned here: to curate — to assemble a series from your own material and to give aesthetic reasons for the selection as well as for the exclusions, under conditions of scarcity. To sound out the dimensions of responsibility in that selection. First towards the image material: it is processed into something that is no longer an image. Everything depicted is taken out of its context and processed into a small piece of a large statistical collection of numbers. Second towards the training energy: the reason we train a LoRA should be able to justify the energy it consumes. And to understand in practice what is fixed in a large image model and what can be attached to it: does the model learn style or content, and does it learn what was defined beforehand, or something else?
technical.limits:
Training takes 1-3 hours

Blocks image generation during training
technical.brief: Train custom LoRA models for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large with your own images.

technical.what: The choice is an adapter that was trained here, the word its images were captioned under, and a few motifs, one motif per line, and each becomes a column. Each column then has four pictures: one from the plain model on the motif alone, one from the plain model with the word in front of it, one with the adapter and the word, and one with the adapter alone. One model with one seed generates all pictures, so what separates two of them is the prompt and the adapter alone.
technical.how: An adapter can drift, as the note "LoRA Explorer" says with Ruiz et al. (2023): the ordinary meaning of a word that stood in the captions can shift along. For a motif outside the adapter's training set, the column shows whether a trained manner carries over to the motif, or whether the adapter brings the subjects of its training set along with it.
technical.brief: One trained adapter, put through four states of the same comparison: the same motif, the same seed and the same model, run with and without the word the adapter was trained under, and with and without the adapter itself.
